title: Verb-final (SOV) word order
explanation: The verb comes at the end of the sentence, after the subject and object, instead of in the middle.
example_native: 私はりんごを食べます。
example_gloss: I apple eat = I eat an apple.
bridge_note: English fixes the verb in the middle (subject-verb-object), so the eat/action word always comes right after "I." Japanese saves it for last — you often don't know what's actually happening in a sentence until the very end.

title: Particles mark grammatical role instead of word order
explanation: Small words after each noun (は, が, を, に, で...) show whether it's the topic, subject, object, location, and so on — word order alone doesn't tell you.
example_native: 友達に手紙を書きます。
example_gloss: Friend-to letter-[object] write = I write a letter to my friend.
bridge_note: English uses prepositions before a noun ("to my friend") and relies on word order for subject/object. Japanese puts a small marker after the noun instead — the role is glued to the word itself, not to where it sits in the sentence.

title: Verbs don't conjugate for person or number
explanation: The same verb form is used whether the subject is I, you, he, she, we, or they — Japanese verbs only change for tense and politeness level, never for who's doing the action.
example_gloss: Eat(s). — could mean I eat, you eat, she eats, they eat, depending on context.
bridge_note: English still marks this a little ("I eat" vs "she eats"), and Portuguese marks it heavily (como/comes/come/comemos). Japanese drops person-marking entirely — the subject is often left unsaid once it's clear from context.

title: I-adjectives conjugate like verbs
explanation: One class of adjectives (ending in い) changes form for past tense and negation on its own, without needing a separate "to be" verb.
bridge_note: English adjectives never change form — you always need a separate verb ("was") to shift tense. Japanese i-adjectives carry the tense themselves, behaving more like a verb than like an English adjective.

title: は marks the topic, が marks the subject — and they're not the same thing
explanation: は introduces what the sentence is about; が marks the grammatical subject of the action. A sentence can have a topic that isn't its subject.
example_gloss: As for elephants, the trunk is long. (topic: elephants; subject of "long": trunk)
bridge_note: English collapses topic and subject into the same word ("elephants have long trunks" — one subject, one role). Japanese can name a topic and then a separate subject within it — a distinction English grammar doesn't really have a slot for.

title: Politeness is built into the verb form itself
explanation: The same action is expressed with a different verb ending depending on how formal the situation is — plain form among friends, polite ます form with strangers or in public.
bridge_note: English signals formality through word choice and tone ("grab a bite" vs "would you care to dine"), never through the verb's grammatical ending. Japanese makes register a fixed grammatical choice on every single verb, not just a style preference.
